input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_title: Implications for auditability, reproducibility, and future extensions
input.section_summary: Discuss how JSON outputs and graph structure support audits and reproducible edits; propose mitigations for identified limitations (improved retrieval, hybrid human–AI review, adaptive graph priors) and outline concrete future extensions (cross-document graphs, larger curated corpora, integration with citation-tracking tools).

output:
General background knowledge: Structured, machine-readable section outputs (for example, JSON records that include explicit fields for prose, cited evidence, and provenance metadata) and an explicit document/section graph can aid auditability and reproducibility by making where assertions originate and how sections depend on one another visible to downstream reviewers and tooling. Because this statement is background-motivated rather than empirically established within this paper, we present it here as design rationale rather than validated fact.

Practical implications for auditability. By emitting each section as a validated JSON object that references the exact evidence items used during generation, the pipeline creates a provenance layer that auditors can traverse programmatically. For example, automated checks can (1) enumerate all unique evidence identifiers cited across a manuscript, (2) surface sections that cite no evidence or that cite the same weak evidence repeatedly, and (3) present a compact map from unsupported assertions to the generator output that produced them. General background knowledge: such programmatic provenance reduces the human effort required to locate candidate errors relative to inspecting unconstrained plain text.

Practical implications for reproducible edits. The section graph encodes dependency relations (parent/child, precedence, citation linkages) that make targeted edits less disruptive. When a reviewer requests a correction to a claim in one node, the scheduler can (a) identify downstream sections that depend on that claim, (b) flag them for re-generation or human review, and (c) re-run only the minimal set of generation steps required to restore consistency. We present this as a proposed workflow component; its effectiveness depends on the fidelity of the dependency annotations and the retrieval pipeline.

Proposed mitigations for identified limitations. Where graph propagation or retrieval failures are likely to introduce error, we propose a layered mitigation strategy:
- Improve retrieval coverage and ranking by expanding the candidate pool and by incorporating simple relevance heuristics (e.g., date and venue filters) before evidence injection. This measure is suggested as an engineering mitigation rather than an evaluated intervention in this work.
- Integrate hybrid human–AI review checkpoints at high-impact nodes (for instance, Methods and Claims subsections). Human verification at these checkpoints can prevent propagation of unsupported assertions across the graph.
- Use adaptive graph priors to reflect confidence: annotate edges with confidence scores derived from evidence matches and model-generation diagnostics; use these scores to prioritize human review and conservative re-generation policies.

Concrete future extensions. We outline practical directions that build on the current pipeline and that are amenable to incremental implementation and evaluation:
- Cross-document graph construction: extend the section graph to span multiple related documents so that shared evidence and conflicting claims are surfaced across a corpus rather than within a single manuscript.
- Larger curated corpora for retrieval: assemble domain-specific, human-curated corpora with explicit metadata to reduce retrieval gaps and improve provenance quality during evidence injection.
- Integration with citation-tracking tools: connect generated references and evidence identifiers to existing indexing and citation-tracking services to enable automated checks for retractions, version changes, and citation validity.
- Interactive authoring tools: provide editors with graph visualizations and one-click re-generation for affected descendant nodes, coupled with diff views of JSON fields to expedite review.

Auditability and tooling implications. The combination of JSON outputs and an explicit section graph shifts the audit burden from free-text forensics to structured validation and selective human inspection. Tooling that exploits this structure can automate many routine checks (schema conformity, missing citations, duplicate evidence) while routing semantic judgments to human reviewers. We frame these as design objectives to guide future tool development rather than as empirically demonstrated outcomes in the current experiments.

Caveats and conservative framing. Because the present work does not include large-scale, cross-domain validation of the audit and reproducibility workflows, the benefits described above remain proposals and engineering priorities. We therefore advocate conservative deployment: require mandatory evidence annotations for factual assertions, enable easy human override of automated decisions, and log all generation runs and retrieval inputs to preserve reproducible execution traces.

Summary. In sum, machine-readable section outputs and an explicit section graph create a practical substrate for auditability and reproducible edits. Realizing their full potential will require improved retrieval resources, human–AI review protocols, and integration with external citation infrastructure; we present these items as concrete, incremental directions for future work.
